comment: The diarisation development stretches: five ten-minute cuts from the four stratified test episodes,
pinned here without a byte of the audio. `scripts/measure-der.ps1 -Cut` (or `lab.ps1 der -Cut`) re-creates
each WAV from the episode at the repository root with the ffmpeg line below and refuses one whose bytes
do not match. Two digests per stretch: sha256 is the whole file, which pins the ffmpeg build as well as
the audio (ffmpeg copies the episode's tags into the WAV header, its own encoder string included);
pcmSha256 is the data chunk alone, which pins the samples. A different ffmpeg that decodes identically
passes on the second and says so; different samples fail.
The cut re-encodes, never `-c copy`: with `-ss` before `-i` ffmpeg seeks sample-accurately only when
transcoding, and snaps to a frame boundary under stream copy. Whether a lossy decode is bit-identical
across ffmpeg versions is unproven, and the pin makes the question moot.
Onsets were chosen by cutting three candidate windows per episode — at 20%, 45% and 70% of its
duration — transcribing each with the ASR, and reading the transcripts for conversation against ad
reads, guests evidently present and speaking, and turn density. That is text-only inference and says
nothing certain about voice count or overlap; the labelling pass is where those become known. The
windows not chosen, and why, are under candidatesNotChosen so a later robustness stretch — an ad read
with the return to conversation after it — can be picked knowingly.
nominalVoices is the EPISODE's speaker count, and as of 2026-08-20 those four counts — 2, 3, 5 and 7 —
are the maintainer's own confirmation rather than an inference from the filenames: no ad-reads and no
jingle voices. What that confirms is the episode. It does not confirm that every one of those voices
speaks inside a given ten-minute window, so on a stretch the number stays an upper bound and the
reference is still what settles it.
The reference for a stretch is <id>.rttm beside this file, made with `uindosill rttm` from an Audacity
label export as README.md describes; the labelled slot below is flipped when it lands. Until then the
stretch is cut and measurable for real-time factor and memory, and not for DER.

ffmpeg.note: The WAV muxer drops the episodes' embedded cover-art stream on its own; no -vn is needed and none was used.

stretches.why: 20% of the episode. Sustained discussion between the two hosts throughout: long turns with back-channel, one question-and-answer run near the end, no ad read and no music in the transcript. The primary two-host stretch, and the first to label.

45% of the episode, chosen to complement two-hosts-a with a different turn character: the first three minutes are a fast-alternating comedic bit (short turns every few seconds), then a one-host schedule read, then discussion. A stress on speaker-change timing rather than on long turns.

70% of the episode. The guest is addressed by name and answers at length across two topics; a mix of quick exchanges and one long turn near the end; no ad read. The 20% window was a near-monologue guest interview with only one host evidently active, and the 45% window had no guest and spent its second half on sponsor copy.

20% of the episode. Two guests are addressed by name and answer; the transcript shows dense cross-talk (several speakers merged into single ASR segments), one longer guest turn, no ad read. Expect the labelling to be slow here — that is the point of the stretch. The 45% window lost its last three minutes to a sponsor read; the 70% window named nobody.

45% of the episode. The densest multi-voice turn-taking of the three windows — short frequent turns, visible interruptions, a floor hand-off by name — with at least two guests named and speaking and no ad read. This is the stretch that prices the four-speaker cap. The 70% window was more than half a solo sponsor read.

candidatesNotChosen.why: Real exchange only in the first two minutes, then a five-minute single-voice explanatory monologue with sparse back-channel.
Clean guest interview, but effectively two active voices: the second host is name-dropped, not heard.
No guest in the window; roughly the back 45% is three sponsor reads with a two-voice tag after each. A candidate for a later ad-read robustness stretch.
One confirmed guest; the last three minutes are a scripted single-voice sponsor read.
Consistently multi-voice and ad-free, but nobody is addressed by name, so the labeller would have no textual anchor for who is who.
Genuine multi-voice interaction, but a single guest monologue occupies the middle third.

About sixty percent solo sponsor read; guests present only in the first two minutes and a twelve-second return at the end. A candidate for a later ad-read robustness stretch, because the return is cross-talk.
